title: Scottish Mixtape Pt. 2 // Cairngorm Traverse
content:
A self-supported mission to link 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks in Scotland.

In partnership with Arc’teryx, Moots Cycles, Tailfin, and Skratch Labs.

Words by KYLE RICHARDSON · Photos by THOMAS WOODSON, KYLE RICHARDSON

TRACK 2:  Cairngorm Traverse

Thomas and I wake to the pitter-patter of rain against the metal roof of the Ben Nevis luxury inn. We are happy to get a good night's rest and sleep inside, but the rain outside challenges our mood and stokes. I like to prescribe to coffee and then take on the day. No use formulating outcomes or stressors on the day till you're fully awake and alert. We are treated downstairs to a classic Scottish breakfast fare and some striking characters. Thomas and I don’t say much to each other this morning. Our crown jewel for this project — Tower Ridge on Ben Nevis stands mysteriously in the clouds, and the rain is picking up.

In these moments, I always wonder what good it does to check in with the weather. It is what it is, right? On this day, the weather gods were against us. Torrential rain, 40- 50 mph winds, and sub-freezing temps. I think we were both wondering if heading up into the cirque was even possible on a day like this, not to mention all the riding we needed to do. Thomas was also starting to show some signs of the previous wet and cold days, developing a minor cold. Still, we don’t speak about the obvious objective and weather challenge.

Dressed and ready for the day, we head down to the hotel's bike storage and start assembling and tinkering with our rigs for the day. There is a door to the outside there that is slightly cracked. I can hear the rain smashing against the door in waves, and gusts of wind occasionally breach this door and rush in. It’s at this point that we start to look at a more detailed forecast. Grim. At this point, it just seems a bit foolish and dumb to force this technical ridge in these conditions. Could we hike up the standard hikers route and summit Ben Nevis? Yes, for sure. That being said, our inspiration lacked for this alternative. So as the rain continued to fall, we biked away from Fort William with no peak.

On trips like this, the timeline doesn’t allow for you to wait on good weather or hunker down. The rest of the mixtape was waiting. I have a love-hate relationship with cruxes on a trip like this. You need to make a decision and get on with it. No point in sulking or being bummed about your current state. I told Thomas we would be back for it someday, and I’m sure he was grateful to focus on the bike for today and his body preservation. Certainly, going up into the Ben with those temperatures and winds would have only sent his body plummeting (and start my downfall too!). Which is totally fair; we have to compromise and make the best of our current situation. As you will find out in the coming paragraphs, we had a wonderful day as we started our traverse of the Cairngorms.

Leaving Fort William on Day 4, the rain only continues. This helps validate our decision. As every day prior, we are quickly into the rough stuff and off-piste trails. As we leave the highlands and start heading East, we assume that maybe today's riding will be slightly less vert-intensive. Only time will tell. An hour into the ride, the skies really open up. The torrential rain meets us a mile or so outside of the tiny village of Spean Bridge. The type of rain you can’t really ride in. Feels proper sketchy. Your first reaction under these conditions is to find shelter. We spot the first cafe and pull in. The sound of rush-hour traffic plowing through pooled-up water on the road keeps us alert. Inside the cafe, we see fellow cyclists and motorists looking soggy and dreary. This is all just part of the unexpected adventure. Going with the twists and turns of the day is what makes an outing rich and rewarding. We both order a big stack of pancakes and tea. Calories usually help keep the good vibes going. Plus, Thomas and I keep a healthy banter going that usually keeps the good times flowing.

Leaving Spean Bridge, we were treated to a brief moment of truly blue skies and sunshine, a first of the trip. As we transitioned from the Highlands and started riding East, we began to ride favorable winds, and the terrain started to shift. As we traversed many a farm field, we began to get a taste of the sneaky gnarly tracks that lie in the rolling hills between the big mountains. The riding here was lush and interesting. We chased sheep around corners and swooped down into grassy fields. To me, this style of riding is quintessential Scotland. Some low country, hard-to-read and faint tracks that really keep you guessing where you are going. We rode by some ancient ruins and crossed a few technical creeks. The riding here is playful and slow. Our bikes are filthy and covered in muck, yet Thomas and I forget about our morning sorrow and worries. We climb beautiful singletrack through a purple haze of heather and twist our way into new zones.

The rain and swirling clouds pick up as we climb towards Lochan na h-Earba. The exposure and grandeur of this place set in. The clouds shift to a darker tone, and Thomas and I space out. We are sandwiched between some peaks, but the atmosphere feels desolate and isolated. No trees or anything for shelter. The rain worsens. I start smashing pedals in hopes of crossing the few miles of this loch to a set of woods on the other side. The double-track here is lined with unavoidable mud and puddles. Franz Ferdinand jamming in my ears, the pedals turn over, and the legs feel good. I look back behind me for the flash of Thomas’s sinewave beacon, letting me know he is on his way. We both reach the safety of the woods in a bit of a blur. The cold has really set in, and Thomas and I comment on how things are getting quite serious. Both soaked to the bone, we know this isn’t a place we can really hang out.

After the wave of storms rolled through, we were rewarded with tailwinds and sunshine. Crossing castles and more lochs, our sights were set on the village of Kingussie. It felt good to stomp out some tarmac and make decent time to our final stop for the day. My classic memory of this day is rolling up on a pair of Highland coos. I will never forget their eyes slowly closing and their hair blowing in the wind. Symbolic of the day we had. Thomas and I were ready for our usual fish n chips entree and then sleep.

Day 5, our routine is starting to find its Scottish rhythm. Having ridden here in 2022, I can confidently say that the riding around Cairngorm National Park is world-class. The network of trails and gravel roads between the River Spey and CNP is amazing. You could spend a couple of weeks exploring and setting a home base in Kingussie or Aviemore. Definitely something I would consider doing sometime in the future. Diving bombing single track and pine needle tracks through quaint neighborhoods had Thomas and me stoked for this new shift in terrain and topography. Skies also looked calm and mostly favorable all day, a real Scottish treat! We stopped to admire ancient castles and babbling brooks. Our chatter flowing and bike cranks spinning.

Rolling into Glenmore National Nature Preserve at the bottom of Cairngorm National Park feels distinctly different than the Highlands. This side of the country feels more arid and dry. There are clusters of woods and trees that make this area feel more like Colorado. We can see the peaks forming above us, their alpine tundra looking distinctly beige and purple. On this day, we were going to be meeting up with a local friend and professional photographer, Johnny Cook. Thomas and I met Johnny at the Kendal Mountain film festival in 2021. We instantly hit it off with Johnny, and we both had just made a friend for life. It was extra special to reunite with him on this trip and have him show us our second ridge of the trip: Fiacaill Ridge.

From Glenmore, it was a roughly 1,000ft climb up to the Cairngorm Mountain and ski hill, our staging zone to start running. I reveled in the 1k tarmac climb, reminiscent of an alpine switchbacked road that we are both familiar with back home. The sun was shining brightly; I took my shirt off for the first time all trip. With the energy from the sun and our excitement to start running, we smashed our way up this climb. The juxtaposition of going from more isolated terrain to a more touristy spot is always a shock, but I have grown used to this dynamic over the many trips in my career. I just embrace the adventure and enjoy the side banter with random folks. We are on our own quest, and it's best not to get overwhelmed by much and stay rock steady.

As Thomas and I were transitioning from cycling shoes to running shoes, our friend Johnny appeared. Our morale was great, but when you see a friend after a long hiatus, our mood and vibe totally skyrocketed. Thomas and I were eager to catch up with Johnny and have him show us one of his local alpine romps. As we started to run, the wind said hello. Okay, maybe it was more of a raging hello! The wind couldn’t dampen our spirits as we started to travel cross-country towards Fiacaill ridge. From far away, this ridge looked unassuming and chill. Up close, the ridge became uniquely geometric and blocky. The granite scrambling here was super unique, and the positioning above the corries (bowl- or amphitheater-shaped hollows carved into the side of mountains by glacial erosion during past ice ages) was dramatic and exposed. The wind tried to blow us off the ridge, but it just added an alpine feeling to it all. Fall colors were beginning to show in the tundra, and the views were panoramic and otherworldly. Johnny does a lot of skiing and works in the ski industry, and he was pointing out all the couloirs and interesting lines. As we ran back down into the corrie, we spotted climbers on more vertical terrain. A subtle reminder for me to come back and do more exploring here. It's always inspiring to get out with a local and really absorb the flavor of a zone.

Back on the bikes, it was another transition and then a mach speed rip back down Cairngorm mountain road to Glenmore. On our way down, we could see the devastation from wildfires that have consumed and burned a lot of the hills surrounding where we were running. From my research online, “The blaze burned approximately 25 square kilometres (around 3,500 football pitches or 2,500 hectares) of rare Caledonian forest, Scots pine, and moorland on July 24th, 2026, prompting the evacuation of over 700 people from areas including Glenmore and Nethy Bridge. Over 500 firefighters, helicopters, and partner agencies fought the blaze.” From what I recall, the embers seep deep into the soil and burn for a while, making it super hard to control and mitigate. Seeing the burned hillsides is sobering and also reminds us of the very similar fire reality we live with back home. Okay, time to keep rolling.

Back down in Glenmore, Thomas and I are ready for some calories. Johnny meets us at the Pine Martin, a ski après-style bar for our post-run hang. We sat there and chatted for a while, eating some delicious curry, enjoying a pint of something light and refreshing. Thomas and I didn’t look at the clock or feel rushed. This was part of our adventure, and our agenda was being created in real time. Soaking up the good times together, not knowing when our paths would cross with Johnny again. When it was time to part ways, Johnny gave us a celebratory sip of a really nice whiskey. As we wet our palates with something way too nice and expensive for Thomas and I ever to own, the sweetness of orchard fruits, baking spices, and smoke dance on our tongues. We say farewell to our Scottish friend and hop back onto the bikes.

Due to the fires I mentioned above, our original plan to go up and over Ryvoan Pass is thwarted by wildfire closures. Moments like this always happen on bikepacking trips, so it's best to just stay calm and not stress about a potential detour or going a new way. In all honesty, I was excited to ride something new; I had done Ryvoan Pass before in 2022. It's really, really cool, but what we ended up doing was equally cool and unique. It was getting to be late afternoon, and Thomas and I were strategizing how far we could make it that evening. As we shredded down some loamy forested tracks, we set our sights on the village of Nethy Bridge; from there we would make our dinner plans and riding goal for the rest of the evening. I always really enjoy getting back on the bike after running. Feels like you end up covering so much ground when using multiple modes of transportation.

In Nethy Bridge, we were coming up on 5 pm. We dashed into a quaint convenience store in an otherwise tiny and quiet town. Inside, it was the usual grab for something salty and sweet. A sip of sugar and chips... oh wait, they call these things crisps. After the pitstop, we got back on track, linking our tracks to the fire detour. The afternoon and early evening were unfolding in good fortune, and hopping between villages kept us psyched and spontaneous. As the purple sky began to meet the purple heather-lined two-track, our stopping point for the evening came into focus: Tomintoul. The segment from Nethy to Tomintoul was a wonderful all-terrain delight. Premier Cairngorm cycling, a bit of an adventure navigating a twisting river, and a dash of hiking. An hour of sunset spinning brought us to a tarmac climb up to our final destination of the day.

Tomintoul felt a bit mysterious and quaint. Less than 800 people call this place home, and only a few spots of sustenance are available. The one place with lights on was the local hotel and Indian food joint. Well, I know what we are having for dinner. What seemed maybe slightly suspect ended up turning into a fine evening of calories. Maybe slightly chaotic for our tired bodies, but it was our only option. After dinner, it was a few-minute spin towards the park above town to find a spot to camp. Thomas and I set up our tarp, donned the midge nets, flicked our red lights on, and tucked into our bivy. A solid day out traversing one of Scotland’s wonderful landscapes!

Stay tuned for Track 3: the Pictish Trail.
